source.title: Model Swarms: Collaborative Search to Adapt LLM Experts via Swarm Intelligence
source.authors: Shang-Bin Feng; Zifeng Wang; Yike Wang; Sayna Ebrahimi; Hamid Palangi; Lesly Miculicich; Achin Kulshrestha; N. Rauschmayr; Ye-Jin Choi; Yulia Tsvetkov; Chen-Yu Lee; Tomas Pfister

page_placements.theme: Multiple weak supervisors: assignment, weighting, boosting, merging and diversity

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or wrong-document issue; the full paper text is present, though some tables and figures are flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites and invokes weak-to-strong generalization, but its own weak-to-strong result uses collaborative weight-space search over existing experts, not a strong student fine-tuned on weak-model labels or PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test weak-supervisor labels or calculate PGR. Its related result is that Model Swarms can use collaborative search to improve weaker starting experts relative to the strongest initial expert; this is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: Model Swarms borrows the weak-to-strong label for a weight-space search in which weaker LoRA experts, guided by a validation-set utility, beat the best initial expert. No strong student is fine-tuned on a weaker model's labels, and no PGR or strong ceiling is measured. Its 'weak-to-strong' results (Appendix B, Figure 9; Figure 3) concern a different construct, so no claim version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say collaborative search brings out the implicit expertise of weak experts, enabling a 'weak-to-strong expert transition'. They describe weak experts as 'diamond in the rough'. This is a framing borrowed from Burns et al., not a test of weak supervision.
record.recipe_differences: The original claim concerns supervised fine-tuning of a strong student on labels from a weak supervisor and uses PGR. This paper searches in model-weight space with a swarm of experts guided by a utility function; it does not use weak-supervisor labels or PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the outcome depends on the diversity of the initial expert pool; it also reports performance across different datasets and swarm compositions.

fits_no_version.finding: With the top-1 initial expert withheld, a swarm of the remaining Gemma-7B LoRA experts exceeds it (reported 35.4% average improvement). A bottom-half swarm exceeds it on 2 of 3 datasets. Separately, 89.6% of ending-best particles did not start as best, and 56.9% started in the bottom half (Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Utility-guided collaborative weight-space search among weaker same-base experts can yield a model exceeding the strongest initial expert on the search objective.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of the 42nd ICML; PMLR 267, 2025)
record.problems: The weak-to-strong evidence is for a different intervention from weak-label fine-tuning, and the cited aggregate result does not specify the four datasets in its prose. Some figure values are not extractable from the flattened text.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results left out. Other Model Swarms results concern adaptation objectives or baselines, not weak-supervisor-label training.

untested.parts: No strong student trained on weak-supervisor labels; no PGR.
No confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembling or loss variants for weak-label training.
No PGR variation across supervisor/student size, task or representations.
No exploitation, distribution-shift or error-overlap analysis for weak-label training.

missing.what: Diamond-in-the-rough statistic: 10.4% of ending-best particles started best; 56.9% started in the bottom half. This is the paper's other weak-to-strong framing; it relates to the fits_no_version finding only.

record.verdict_notes: Weak-to-strong here means weak initial experts collectively surpassing the best expert under ground-truth utility guidance. This differs fundamentally from weak-label supervision. The prose says 'four datasets' while Figure 9 shows three; the 35.4% figure cannot be checked against flattened figure values.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on weak-supervisor labels and no PGR measurement.
No auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembling, or loss-variant comparison for weak-label fine-tuning.
No PGR comparison across supervisor/student sizes, task types, or representations.
No tests of weak-label exploitation, distribution shift in weak-label training, or error overlap between weak and strong models.
No theoretical conditions for a student trained on weak labels to beat its supervisor.
No weak-label student-supervisor test in vision or another non-language modality.

relation.reason: The paper cites Burns et al. and applies weak-to-strong terminology to collaborative expert search; it does not operationally use weak-label supervision.

tranche.reason: The method uses particle swarm optimization and validation-set utility, not the catalogued weak-supervision finding as a tool. Its expert-composition results measure a different construct and test no claim version.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. The prose reports 35.4% across four datasets, while Figure 9 names only three: MMLU, Hellaswag and NLGraph; the fourth dataset is unresolved.
